summary: Describes how the TIFF image format is used to represent image data for black-and-white and color fax, as specified by ITU-T recommendations. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 3949.

eli5.summary: Fax machines send pictures of pages. This memo explains how to save those pictures in a common picture file type that computers understand.

questions: tiff file format for internet fax
how is fax image data stored in tiff
subtitle: How to store fax images using the TIFF file format.

tldr.problem: Fax machines send and receive black-and-white, grayscale, and color documents, but there was no standard way to store fax image data in computer files for email and archival. Each application used its own format.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2301 defines TIFF-FX: a specification for storing fax image data in the TIFF (Tag Image File Format) image file format. It defines six profiles (S, F, J, C, L, M) for different types of fax (black-and-white, lossless, color, etc.), each with specific compression methods and TIFF field requirements.
tldr.outcome: Internet fax applications can now exchange fax documents as TIFF files with standardized compression, resolution, and metadata, compatible with ITU-T fax standards. It was refined by RFC 3949.

today: RFC 2301 was obsoleted by RFC 3949, which is the current standard for TIFF-FX. Internet fax applications continue to use TIFF-FX format for storing and exchanging fax images, though email-based fax services often use other formats like PDF or JPEG for web compatibility.

sections.title: Why TIFF for Fax
sections.content:
Facsimile (fax) machines have used standardized protocols for decades, defined by ITU-T recommendations. However, when Internet fax applications needed to store fax images in files (for email, archival, or store-and-forward services), there was no standard file format. RFC 2301 solves this by defining how to use TIFF (Tag Image File Format), a well-established image format, to store fax image data.

TIFF is ideal for fax because it supports multi-page documents, multiple compression methods, and detailed metadata. RFC 2301, known as TIFF-FX, defines which TIFF fields and compression methods must be used to make fax files that comply with ITU-T fax standards and can be exchanged between different applications.
sections.eli5: Fax machines have rules for how to send pages over phone lines. This RFC lets you save those faxes in a standard picture file format so computers can store and share them.

sections.title: TIFF File Structure for Fax
sections.content:
TIFF files consist of an 8-byte header, followed by one or more Image File Directories (IFDs). Each IFD represents one image (or page) and contains metadata fields that describe the image: dimensions, resolution, compression method, color encoding, and pointers to the actual image data. A multi-page fax document is represented as a linked list of IFDs, one per page, with the first IFD pointing to the second, and so on.

The image data itself is stored in strips—blocks of compressed image data. A single page may use one strip or multiple strips (to reduce memory requirements). The StripOffsets and StripByteCounts fields in the IFD tell the reader where each strip is located and how long it is after compression.

Essential fields required for all fax modes include ImageWidth and ImageLength (dimensions), XResolution and YResolution (resolution in pixels per inch or centimeter), Compression (the compression method used), and PhotometricInterpretation (what pixel values mean: black or white, or color components).
sections.eli5: A TIFF file is like a filing cabinet. The header points to the first page's drawer. Each drawer (IFD) has labels describing the image: its width, height, how many dots per inch, and how the picture is compressed. The labels also point to where the actual picture data lives in the file.

sections.title: Fax Profiles and Compression Methods
sections.content:
RFC 2301 defines six profiles, each for a different type of fax document:

Profile S (Minimal black-and-white): Binary black-and-white fax using Modified Huffman (MH) compression. All implementations must support this. Fixed width of 1728 pixels (North American Letter or ISO A4). Resolutions of 200 or 204 pixels per inch horizontally, and 98 to 200 pixels per inch vertically.

Profile F (Extended black-and-white): Black-and-white fax with higher resolutions and two additional compression methods: Modified Read (MR) and Modified Modified Read (MMR), defined in ITU-T Recommendations T.4 and T.6. Supports variable widths and resolutions.

Profile J (Lossless JBIG black-and-white): Modern lossless compression (JBIG) for black-and-white images, providing better compression than MH or MR.

Profile C (Lossy color and grayscale): Color and grayscale fax using JPEG compression. Lossy compression means the image is not perfectly reconstructed, but provides smaller files.

Profile L (Lossless color and grayscale): Color and grayscale fax using JBIG compression for lossless representation.

Profile M (Mixed Raster Content): Combines multiple compression methods in a single document, allowing text (with lossless compression) and photographs (with lossy compression) on the same page.

All color implementations must support Profile C; implementations of other profiles must also support all profiles on the path connecting them to Profile S (the root).
sections.eli5: Different kinds of faxes need different compression. Simple black-and-white text compresses one way, modern lossless works better with another way, and color photos need yet another. The RFC defines a profile (a set of rules) for each type of fax.

sections.title: Image Data, Compression, and Resolution
sections.content:
Image data is stored as a stream of compressed data within strips. The compression method is specified in the Compression field of the IFD, and the compressed data follows ITU-T standards. The compression parameters (such as the state machine settings for Modified Huffman) are embedded in the compressed data stream itself, not in TIFF fields, which allows TIFF to be independent of specific compression standards.

Fax documents have precise resolution requirements. Horizontal resolution is typically 200 or 204 pixels per inch (dpi), while vertical resolution ranges from 98 dpi (standard) to 200 dpi (fine) or higher. The XResolution and YResolution fields record these values.

One important detail is bit order. The FillOrder field indicates how bits are stored within bytes. Traditional fax equipment transmits bits with the least significant bit first (LSB), so most fax implementations use FillOrder=2 to match this convention, even though Baseline TIFF uses most significant bit first.

The T4Options field (used with Modified Huffman compression) specifies whether EOL (End of Line) codes are byte-aligned, which helps readers avoid bit-shifting when processing scan lines.
sections.eli5: The actual picture data is squeezed down using a compression method, and the compression stays compressed in the file. The TIFF labels say what resolution the picture is (how many dots per inch), which direction the bits go in, and whether line endings are on byte boundaries.

sections.title: Multi-Page Documents and Implementation
sections.content:
A multi-page fax document in TIFF-FX is a linked list of IFDs. The PageNumber field in each IFD contains two values: the page number (starting from 0) and the total page count. This lets readers know how many pages to expect and which page they are reading.

The NewSubFileType field marks each IFD as a page of a multi-page document (by setting Bit 1 to 1). A new GlobalParametersIFD field can appear in the first IFD to provide global fax parameters (like the fax profile type and coding methods used in the file) in one convenient location, rather than requiring the reader to scan through all pages.

RFC 2301 recommends a specific ordering of pages and elements within a page to simplify implementation and enable streaming of fax data. Minimal black-and-white mode (Profile S) requires single-strip images (one strip per page) and little-endian byte order (header value II) for maximum compatibility.

Readers must handle potential discrepancies between values stored in the compressed data stream and values in TIFF fields. When interpreting the actual image data, the values in the compressed stream take precedence, while TIFF field values are informational.
sections.eli5: Each page of a multi-page fax is labeled with its page number. You can put a label at the beginning that says which compression methods the whole file uses and which rules it follows. The format recommends a specific way to arrange pages so different programs can handle fax files the same way.
